source_ref: osf.io/5e9y3 Codebook.xlsx, sheet "Study 1" -- it keys every it.* variable to its administered item text, its trait/subscale, and its response scale; study1-maindat.csv for the response columns; data/sun_2025_morality.do for the code derivation. Sun, Wu & Goodwin (2025), 'Are moral people happier?', doi:10.1037/pspp0000539.
note: CORRECTS THIS TABLE'S FIRST EXTRACTION IN THIS SAME BATCH, on both axes. The first pass took wording from the deposit's normdat-labels.csv, whose ids carry an `mv.` prefix, and reasoned that mv.X.Fn and it.X.Fn were the same item 'differing only in the rater-frame prefix'. They are not the same rendering: `mv.` is the TRAIT-NORMING study's measured-variable label set, whose entries are deliberately stem-less fragments for a norming task ('is a fair person'), while the live codes come from Study 1's informant-report `it.` variables. It also recorded that 'the deposit and the paper do not state what the five points were labelled', which was wrong. Codebook.xlsx sheet "Study 1" carries BOTH the administered item text and a per-item response scale, and is now the source for both. The correspondence is mechanical and one-to-one, not inferred: study1-maindat.csv's header is literally 'it.MCQ.F1', Stata's import delimited strips the dots (illegal in a Stata name) and data/sun_2025_morality.do then does `rename *, lower`, yielding itmcqf1. NOTE ON THE PLACEHOLDERS: the codebook renders the piped fields literally as [target's name] and [he/she/they], and they are kept verbatim rather than resolved or stripped -- that is the item as the codebook documents it, and respondents saw the target's actual name and pronouns in those slots. The codebook's own typographic apostrophe was normalised to ASCII (it is inconsistent within the sheet, straight in one row and curly in another). The codebook's "INFORMANT-REPORT" line is a document heading, not an administered stem, so section_prompt is left empty. The scale for this block is stated as '1 = Strongly disagree, 2 = Disagree, 3 = Neither agree nor disagree, 4 = Agree, 5 = Strongly agree' and is identical across all four items. Note it differs from the sibling fairnessHEXACO table at point 3, which the codebook gives as 'Neutral (neither agree nor disagree)' -- the two blocks were administered with different midpoint wording and are recorded as such rather than harmonised.
public_note: Informant ratings of a target person on the Moral Character Questionnaire's Fairness facet, answered 1 (Strongly disagree) to 5 (Strongly agree). Item text keeps the codebook's [target's name] placeholder; respondents saw the actual name. itmcqf3 is reverse-worded and is stored RAW.

source_ref: osf.io/4b85w data paper/codebooks/processed_data_dictionary.csv (Variable, Section Header, Field_Type, Field_Label, possible values) -- Oxford ARC study; Parsons, Todorovic, Lim, Songco & Fox (2022) data and protocol paper
note: Level-1 source with no mapping inference at all. The Oxford ARC data paper ships codebooks/processed_data_dictionary.csv, one row per variable; every item code here appears in its Variable column verbatim, item_text is that row's Field_Label and section_prompt its Section Header. The codes are self-describing besides (media_why_tv_news), so a permutation could not survive a reading. SCOPE CHANGED, see #1996 and PR #2008: this table originally carried 44 items on two response formats, but the 8 'text' items were free-text average-hours-per-day quantities rather than scale responses and are being dropped from the response table, so their 48 rows are removed here and the surviving section is renumbered _2 -> _1. What remains is one format and one section: 36 'radio' items under 'please rate how much you did this activity for the following reasons', each carrying all five labels '1, Never | 2, Rarely | 3, Sometimes | 4, Often | 5, Always'. option_text is now populated on all 180 rows. instructions is empty because the dictionary gives no whole-table framing distinct from that section header. audit_batch.R WARNed on the 44-item version; both halves of that WARN are resolved or explained -- the blank-option_text half was the hours items and is gone, and the row-count half is the instrument, not a defect: the 36 reason items fall into six clusters of six with near-identical n inside each (2,264-2,304 up to 6,193-6,277) because each medium's six reasons were shown only to respondents who used that medium. audit_report.csv is left as the generated record of the audit that actually ran, against the 44-item live table; it cannot be re-run cleanly until PR #2008 is merged and the response table re-uploaded.
public_note: 36 items, each rated 1 = Never to 5 = Always. Six reasons for use (socialise, fun, news, work, avoidance, nothing else to do) crossed with six media. Each medium's six reasons were shown only to respondents who reported using that medium, so item n varies by medium.

note: The three additional questions are reproduced verbatim in the article's S1 File under 'Part 4 : Additional questions', followed by 'Participants gave a single answer to each item.' source_ref: Gratz & Roemer (2004), 'Multidimensional Assessment of Emotion Regulation and Dysregulation', J Psychopathol Behav Assess 26:41-54, Table III (all 36 items) and p.44 (response anchors); item codes and used resp levels from the live table; DERS_SUM_POST from the deposit, osf.io/9jgxs 'amps psychometric eval.csv'. Study paper: 10.1007/s12671-023-02144-1 (PMC12959836).
note: Wording is the instrument's own publication; the mapping is reconstructed and verified on three routes (see verify_paampsmartsud_saba_2023_ders.R). THE NUMBERING TRAP: Table III numbers items in the original 41-item pool, not the published 36-item numbering the deposit uses. Pool items 2, 11, 13, 18 and 36 were dropped and the survivors renumbered 1..36 in ascending order; shipping Table III's numbers as-is would have misassigned most of the scale. That renumbering is what was tested: it places the article's 11 reverse-scored items on exactly positions 1, 2, 6, 7, 8, 10, 17, 20, 22, 24, 34, which the deposit's own DERS_SUM_POST independently pins (dropping DERS_37_POST and reversing those 11 reproduces the total for all 90 complete rows, where no other single-column drop exceeds 42 of 90 and no-reverse scoring matches 6). DERS_37_POST is therefore NOT a scored DERS item and its wording is unknown, so it ships with empty item_text and empty option_text rather than being guessed; its resp rows are present so the item and resp sets still match the live table. DEVIATIONS: two PDF rendering artefacts were normalised in the text -- the fi/fl ligatures (U+FB01/U+FB02) to ASCII, and the typographic apostrophe (U+2019) to "'" -- neither is a feature of the administered form. Response anchors are Gratz & Roemer's own, including their percentage bands; note that the study paper renders the low anchor as 'never' where the instrument's publication says 'almost never (0-10%)', and the instrument was followed. No administered instruction text was recovered from either the deposit or the two papers, so instructions and section_prompt are empty; the study describes a 30-day reporting window and Gratz & Roemer describe the task as indicating 'how often the items apply to themselves', but neither reproduces what respondents were shown. RIGHTS: cleared under the corrected test settled in #1945 -- the DERS carries no licence fee and no quotable no-redistribution clause (APA PsycTests 10.1037/t01029-000 is behind SSO and could not be quoted either way), so silence is permission. Supersedes this table's earlier blocked note, which was held partly on the superseded stricter reading. On DERS_37_POST specifically: it is not identifiable, but it does sit in the same administered matrix -- n = 180 responses and an observed range of 1-5, identical to all 36 scored items, with mean 1.86. That is why its resp rows are kept; the option labels are still left blank rather than inferred from the block, since an unidentified item could carry its own anchors.
public_note: The 36-item Difficulties in Emotion Regulation Scale administered post-intervention. resp runs 1-5 over Gratz & Roemer's anchors, stored RAW -- the 11 reverse-keyed items (DERS_1, _2, _6, _7, _8, _10, _17, _20, _22, _24, _34_POST) are not pre-reversed, so reverse them before summing. DERS_37_POST is in the response table but is not a scored DERS item and its wording is not recorded anywhere in the deposit or the papers; it ships with no item text rather than a guess. Its observed responses do span 1-5 with the same respondent count as the scored items, so it appears to have been administered on the same grid.

source_ref: Deposit SPSS file 'Data_main experiment_13 countries_July 2 2024.sav' (the file behind the dictionary's OSF view_only link, supplied directly), variable labels NFC_1-NFC_5 and their value labels; data/pezzuti_2025_coolpeople.do for the code derivation. Article: Pezzuti, Warren & Chen (2025), 'Cool People', J Exp Psychol Gen, 10.1037/xge0001799.
note: Level-1 extraction, no mapping inference. The .sav carries a variable label per item, and data/pezzuti_2025_coolpeople.do does `rename *, lower` and then `gen item = "`var'"`, so the live code nfc_1-nfc_5 IS the lowercased source column name. Each label is a shared stem plus the item, split on ' - ': the stem became section_prompt and the remainder item_text. CORRECTS THIS TABLE'S EARLIER BLOCKED NOTE, which called the five items a Need for Cognition short form -- that was a guess from the code name and it is wrong. The items are about rules, instructions and standardized work procedures. They are the uncertainty-avoidance dimension of the CVSCALE: the article states that in the initial samples it 'included items to measure beliefs about cultural dimensions' citing Yoo et al. (2011), and all five wordings match CVSCALE's uncertainty-avoidance items. That identification comes from the citation plus the wording match, NOT from any source that keys these codes to a named dimension, and the study's own materials never name it -- they only label the block NFC. Note also that CVSCALE is normally administered on 5 points and this study used 7. ANCHORS: the .sav value labels read 'strongly disagree1' and 'strongly agree7' -- Qualtrics appended the scale number, which was stripped. Points 2-6 carry no label in the source and are left blank rather than padded with their own number. The typographic apostrophe in item 1 was normalised to ASCII. COVERAGE: only 844 of the 3,972 respondents in the live table answered this block, which matches the article -- these were exploratory measures run only in the initial samples. RIGHTS: clears the corrected test in #1945. No fee or no-redistribution clause is quotable for the CVSCALE. The article PDF does carry an APA notice that it 'is not to be disseminated broadly', but that governs the article, not the instrument, and no wording here was taken from the article -- it all comes from the study's own .sav.
public_note: Five uncertainty-avoidance items, answered on a 7-point agree/disagree scale whose endpoints alone were labelled in the source. Only 844 of the 3,972 respondents saw this block: it was an exploratory measure administered in the initial samples only, so most ids have no response. The item codes read 'nfc' but the items are not a Need for Cognition measure.

THE LIVE TABLE POOLS BOTH STUDIES: IRS1.sav N=618 and IRS 2.sav N=852 sum to the 1,470 live ids, and cov_study marks which. That matters for the anchors, because the two administrations labelled the scale differently: study 1 used 'Neither agree nor disagree' at point 3 and 'Strongly agree' at 5, study 2 used 'Neutral' and 'Strongly Agree'. public_note: Eleven behavioral-avoidance items adapted to ethnic/racial groups, answered 1 (Strongly disagree) to 5 (Strongly agree). The table pools the paper's two studies -- see cov_study. The two studies rendered the midpoint differently ('Neither agree nor disagree' in study 1, 'Neutral' in study 2); the shipped option_text uses study 1's wording throughout, so the point-3 and point-5 labels are exact for study 1 and differ cosmetically for study 2.

source_ref: OSF osf.io/yhu4t, 'CPG CMORR Codebook.pdf' -- BOTH its variable table (p.12) and its prose Measures section, which is where the decisive detail is; supplemental PDF for reported composite statistics. Hughes, Jacobson, Rule & Srivastava (2025).
note: SUPERSEDES THIS TABLE'S EARLIER BLOCKED NOTE, which said the codebook settled 2 of the 12 items. It settles 6, and the reason the first pass undercounted is that it read the codebook's variable table and not its prose Measures section. The prose states the consumer block is SIX items and enumerates all six wordings, and it supplies the composite statistics that pin which code is which. THE FOUR ce CODES: live has ce1, ce2, ce4, ce5 with ce3 absent, against a codebook that names the measures cred_pers and cred_bus, so the codes had to be identified from data. Credibility of the person is reported as the average of 'I believe this person's story' and 'I think I got an incomplete or inaccurate story' (reversed) with M = 4.59, SD = 0.71, alpha = .66. Of all 12 ordered pairs of the four codes, only ce1 with reversed ce2 reproduces it (M = 4.59, SD = 0.70); the opposite orientation gives M = 1.41, so the direction is pinned too, and no other pair comes within 0.4 on the mean. Our alpha is .72 against the reported .66, which is the one loose end -- likely a different analysis subset, since M and SD agree to two decimals. That leaves ce4 and ce5 as the business items, and nps separates them: r(ce4, nps) = +0.447 and r(ce5, nps) = -0.572, so ce4 is 'I would be willing to patronize the business this person described' and ce5 is 'I would tell other people to avoid this business'. Content agrees -- these are consumer COMPLAINT stories, so willingness to patronize is low (M = 2.48) and telling others to avoid is high (M = 3.42). AFFIL6 IS NOT PART OF THE AFFILIATION SCALE. The codebook calls Interest in Affiliation 'this five-item scale' and reports M = 3.98, SD = 0.87, alpha = .93, but the live table carries six affil codes. Dropping affil6 gives alpha = .932, M = 3.97, SD = 0.87 -- the best of all six possible drops on alpha (next best .910) and a two-decimal match on all three statistics. affil6 also has the lowest mean correlation with the rest (0.495 against 0.656-0.725). Its identity is unknown, so no instrument is claimed for it. WHY SIX ITEMS SHIP BLANK: for the five-item affiliation scale the codebook gives only two example wordings ('I like this person', 'I would enjoy spending time with this person') and does not key them to codes, so any per-code assignment would be a guess; affil1-affil5 and affil6 therefore carry no item_text. Tackman & Srivastava (2016) is the cited source and could supply the five wordings, but not an order to key them by, so that would not unblock them either. Their response anchors DO ship. TWO SOURCE CONTRADICTIONS recorded rather than resolved silently: (1) the prose says the affiliation items ran 'from 1 (disagree strongly) to 7 (agree strongly)' while the variable table says 1-5 and the live data contains only 1-5, so the 7 is taken as an error and the endpoint WORDING is used; (2) the variable table gives the NPS item as 'How likely is it that you would recommend this product or company to a friend or colleague?' while the prose gives the longer 'the product or company this person just told you about' -- the prose version ships, being presented as the question asked. NPS live resp runs 1-11 and is the codebook's 0-10 shifted by one. WORDING SEARCH NOW CLOSED, and the answer is that it is published nowhere. The whole deposit was enumerated: osf.io/yhu4t holds four root files (the codebook, the preregistration, the JPSP supplemental, and a Data-and-Code folder) and that folder holds only scored CSVs and Rmd/HTML analysis outputs -- no survey instrument and no labelled data file. The preregistration ('Interpersonal Consequences of Socioeconomic Status', osf.io/download/25s8v) describes the scale as 'a five-item scale to assess interest to affiliate with a previously unknown interaction partner' and says it 'will be calculated as an average of these 5 items', giving NO item wording at all -- not even the codebook's two examples. Grepping every deposit file for the two example wordings returns hits only in the codebook. So the codebook's unkeyed 'e.g.' pair is the only affiliation wording that exists in the record, and affil1-affil6 stay blank. AFFIL6 IS NOW PROVEN FROM THE AUTHORS' OWN SCORING, which supersedes the reliability argument. 'SES stereotypes_scored data.csv' in the deposit ships affil1-affil6 alongside a scored `affil` composite column: averaging the five items with affil6 DROPPED reproduces that composite exactly for all 1,211 complete rows, where averaging all six matches only 221 and no other single-item drop exceeds 565. That is the authors' own scoring decision, not an inference from it. ALSO TRACED: the 1-7 versus 1-5 scale contradiction originates in the preregistration, which states 1 (disagree strongly) to 7 (agree strongly); the codebook copied it. The administered form and the live data both carry only 1-5, so the 7 is a documentation error propagated forward, and the endpoint wording is kept with the 1-5 range taken from the data. THE FIVE AFFILIATION WORDINGS ARE NOW KNOWN, BUT STILL NOT KEYABLE TO CODES. The cited source is Tackman & Srivastava (2016), 'Social responses to expressive suppression: the role of personality judgments', JPSP 110(4), 574, psycnet.apa.org/fulltext/2015-37763-001.pdf, which states: 'We chose the five items by reviewing affiliation items used by Butler et al. (2003) and Gross and John (2003) and using or adapting ones that were appropriate for a zero-acquaintance study. The five items were as follows: (a) "I like this person"; (b) "I would enjoy talking to this person"; (c) "I would enjoy spending time with this person"; (d) "This person is the type of person I could get along with"; (e) "This person is the type of person I could become close friends with". Participants indicated their agreement or disagreement with each item on a scale ranging from 1 (disagree strongly) to 7 (agree strongly).' Two things follow. FIRST, this explains the 1-7 contradiction at its root: the 1-7 is Tackman & Srivastava's ORIGINAL scale, copied into Hughes's preregistration and then into the codebook, while Hughes administered a 5-point version -- which the codebook's own variable table says (1-5), which the live data confirms (only 1-5 present), and which matches every other measure in that study. The shipped endpoint labels are now sourced rather than assumed: Tackman & Srivastava's anchor words are 'disagree strongly' and 'agree strongly'. SECOND, and the reason item_text stays EMPTY: the wordings are known as a SET but their assignment to affil1-affil5 individually is not. Route 4 proves the set (the deposit's own composite averages exactly these five, excluding affil6). The order does not follow. The deposit's column order matching the article's (a)-(e) enumeration is only a convention, and the one discriminating test available comes out AGAINST it: items (d) and (e) share the stem 'This person is the type of person I could ...', so (d) should correlate more with (e) than (c) does, yet r(affil3, affil5) = 0.777 exceeds r(affil4, affil5) = 0.723, which would make affil3 = (d) and reverse the article order. That test is confounded -- affil3's mean (3.892) sits closer to affil5's (3.395) than affil4's (4.101) does, and items closer in difficulty correlate more highly whatever their wording -- so it does not settle the reverse either. Differential correlations with perceived warmth, agreeableness, extraversion and competence separate affil3 from affil4 by at most 0.02. The means do support (a) at affil1 and (e) at affil5, the highest and lowest, but pinning the ends is not pinning the middle, and shipping two items with swapped text is worse than shipping none. WHAT WOULD CLOSE IT: the administered Qualtrics form, which the deposit does not contain. That is a human action -- author contact -- not another statistical route.
public_note: Interpersonal judgements from a round-robin design: each row is one perceiver rating one target, so read it with `rater`. TWO THINGS TO KNOW. First, affil6 is NOT part of the five-item Interest in Affiliation scale -- averaging all six will not reproduce the paper's reported alpha of .93; averaging affil1-affil5 does. This is not a guess: the deposit's own scored data file carries a scored `affil` composite, and dropping affil6 reproduces it exactly for all 1,211 complete rows. affil6's identity is not recorded anywhere in the deposit. Second, the six affil codes ship without item text because the codebook publishes only two unkeyed example wordings for the scale; their 1-5 response anchors are given. The six consumer-experience items all carry verified wording. ce2 and ce5 are reverse-keyed and are stored RAW. NPS resp runs 1-11, which is the original 0-10 shifted by one. The five affiliation items ARE known, from the scale's source (Tackman & Srivastava, 2016, JPSP 110(4), 574), and in the article's order they are: (a) "I like this person"; (b) "I would enjoy talking to this person"; (c) "I would enjoy spending time with this person"; (d) "This person is the type of person I could get along with"; (e) "This person is the type of person I could become close friends with". They are deliberately NOT written into item_text, because which code carries which of the five is not established -- the deposit's column order is only a convention and the available tests do not confirm it. Treat the five as an unordered set covering affil1-affil5. Note also that the codebook and preregistration describe a 1-7 scale; that is the ORIGINAL scale from Tackman & Srivastava, whereas this study administered 5 points, which is what the variable table and the data both show.
